definition: State orientation is a tendency to become stuck in failure-related, uncontrollable thoughts and to hesitate when facing difficult intentions, rather than disengaging and taking action toward another goal. In action control theory, it is described as a vulnerability under stress because it reflects reduced ability to keep goal-directed, self-controlled action going in demanding conditions.

reasons: The definition’s first sentence is supported: the packet defines state orientation as excessive preoccupation with uncontrollable, failure-related thoughts (rumination) instead of action-oriented disengagement, and hesitation rather than action-oriented initiative regarding difficult intentions to reach an alternatively intended goal.

The definition’s second sentence includes a claim that it is “described as a vulnerability under stress because it reflects reduced ability to keep goal-directed, self-controlled action going in demanding conditions.” The packet supports that Action Control Theory treats action vs. state orientation as an organismic resilience vs. risk factor related to stress-dependent symptom formation/maintenance/recovery, but it does not explicitly state the specific “vulnerability under stress” rationale or the particular formulation of “reduced ability to keep goal-directed, self-controlled action going” in demanding conditions.

The definition adds or shifts wording beyond the packet by saying state orientation involves “rather than disengaging and taking action toward another goal”; the source instead describes “excessive preoccupation with uncontrollable, failure-related thoughts” and “hesitation instead of action-oriented initiative” toward an alternatively intended goal.

The phrase “vulnerability under stress” is defensible, but the packet frames state orientation more specifically as an organismic resilience/risk factor that moderates or mediates symptom formation, maintenance, and recovery, so the definition should not generalize beyond that source-specific framing.
